title: Getting started
heading: Getting started
text: Install fleet and create your config: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RolfKoenders/fleet/main/install.sh | sh fleet new ~/fleet-config The new repo is a commented example with placeholder skills and MCP servers. Ask your agent to run fleet agent and follow the onboarding recipe, or edit hosts/ and catalog/ yourself. fleet init fails until the placeholders are gone. Publish it as a private repo: cd ~/fleet-config git add -A && git commit -m "Start my fleet config" gh repo create fleet-config --private --source . --remote origin --push Set up this machine, using its name from hosts/. Init prints an age key once, so save it in your password manager: cd ~/fleet-config fleet init laptop Then add your other machines from this one: fleet init server

title: Getting started
heading: Working with fleet
text: Working with fleet Change the config, check the result, and publish it: fleet diff fleet push -m "Add a skill" fleet push applies the change on every machine with an ssh: line in its host file. Every machine also pulls and applies by itself on a timer, every 30 minutes by default, and timer: in a host file or the defaults changes that. On a terminal it shows each host's progress live and leaves a summary; piped, it prints one timestamped line per host start and result. Command What it does fleet status Report this machine; --all asks every machine over ssh; --conflicts lists this machine's conflicts in full, reading only fleet bridge [--view <screen>] [--host <name>] The full-screen view of every host (needs a terminal), optionally opened on a screen and a host; pushes and doctor only on your confirmation. See the bridge fleet ui [--port <n>] [--no-open] Open a page in your browser to see and search what every host gets, add, edit and remove MCP servers, skill sources, bundles and hosts, set secrets, and push with live progress; it listens on 127.0.0.1 only and stops after 10 minutes with no page open. See the page fleet card [--style machines\ map] [--names] [--badge] Write fleet-card.svg (1200 x 630), an image of your fleet to share: its counts, each machine with its agents and OS, and a year of changes; hosts are host 1, host 2 unless --names, and no server, skill, source or secret name is ever on it. --badge writes a small fleet-badge.svg for a README instead. It reads what fleet last saw of each host and asks none. See the page fleet doctor Start this machine's MCP servers, check each answers and measure how large its tools are (saved as the doctor result); --all asks every machine over ssh. Runs commands with real credentials and may download packages, so it runs only when you ask fleet context Show how much each agent on this machine loads before the first prompt (instructions, skill descriptions, MCP tool definitions) as coloured bars and an estimate in tokens, with the largest items; --all asks every machine over ssh and draws all the bars on one scale, so you can see which machine carries the most. MCP sizes come from the last fleet doctor; reads only, starts no server fleet diff Show what an apply would change fleet apply Make this machine match its config fleet push Publish the config and apply it; --host <name> applies only on that host fleet undo [--no-push] [--yes] [<commit>] Revert the last recorded push, or a named one, and push the revert to the same scope; --no-push stops after the revert commit, --yes skips the prompt fleet adopt Take ownership of an MCP server or skill that already matches fleet secrets Edit, set or rekey encrypted secrets fleet skills update Move pinned skill sources to their latest commit; --review shows what changed first and asks per source fleet update Move the pinned tool version to the newest release (or the latest commit of a branch, see track in fleet.yaml) and print what changed fleet demo Try the bridge on made-up hosts in a throwaway sandbox; --shell gives a shell instead fleet agent Print what an agent needs to know, including task recipes Add --json to any command for output a script can read. Reading a skill update before it moves A skill is instructions your agents follow, so a third-party update changes what they do. fleet skills update --review [<source>] reads each pinned source that would move, without moving anything, and reports the commits between the pins, each skill you use that changed with its diff size (other changed skills are only counted), and what to look at: acme-skills  c19e2a1 → 7d04f6b, 14 commits, 6 of your 38 skills changed (3 others)    ~ grilling                 +12 −3   ! diagnose  scripts/trace.sh   new script; new URL https://…   ! tdd       SKILL.md           allowed-tools: + Bash(curl:*)   i triage    SKILL.md           description changed Warnings (!) are a file with the exec bit, a new script, a new URL, a new bash or sh code block in SKILL.md, a change to allowed-tools, and a new hooks or settings file. A changed description is info (i), because it changes when the skill triggers. The flags are a reading aid, not a verdict. On a terminal it then asks for each source: d shows the full diff of the skills you use, y moves the pin, n keeps it. Without a terminal, or with --json, it only reports, and a pin moves only with --yes. Followed sources are never reviewed. To review a source every time without typing --review, put review: true on it in catalog/skills.yaml. Switch it on for skills other people write and leave it off for your own: a plain fleet skills update then reviews the first and moves the second as before. Only a pinned source can have it.

title: Setting up machines
heading: What each machine needs
text: What each machine needs The machine you work from reaches the others over SSH with a key and no prompt. ssh <destination> true should succeed without asking anything. Put the destination in the machine's host file as its ssh: line. Every machine pulls from and pushes to your config repo, at the address the repo has on the machine you work from. fleet init hands that address to each new machine. A machine with only HTTPS access to GitHub needs a git setting to reach an SSH address: git config --global url."https://github.com/you/".insteadOf "git@github.com:you/"

title: Setting up machines
heading: Which agents a machine gets
text: Which agents a machine gets A machine gets the agents installed on it. Fleet looks for each agent's program (claude, opencode, agy) on the usual paths, in the shims of mise (~/.local/share/mise/shims) and in the directory of the Node that fleet runs under, where npm -g puts agent CLIs. A program in ~/.local/bin is preferred to a shim. Install an agent and the next apply sets it up. An agent that is not installed is left alone: nothing of its is written, and what fleet applied for it earlier stays where it is. An agent you never had is never mentioned, however many agents the shared config names. One you had, and fleet applied config for, is mentioned, so that a lost install does not go unnoticed: warning opencode: not installed, its config is left as is. Install it, or pin `agents:` To choose instead of detect, name the agents in the machine's host file. The list replaces the defaults' list, and a named agent is set up whether or not it is installed (Claude's MCP servers still wait for claude, because they are written through it): agents: [claude] fleet status shows what a machine gets, as agents: claude 2.1.4 (opencode not installed), and fleet context and fleet doctor cover only those agents. fleet status, status --json and the bridge name an agent only on a machine that has it installed, names it in agents:, or applied config for it, so one you never used is not mentioned. status --json keeps the claude and opencode keys in tools as they were (null when not found); any other agent has its key only where it is named. Antigravity CLI Antigravity CLI (agy) keeps its files in ~/.gemini, a folder Gemini CLI uses too. Fleet only touches ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli, ~/.gemini/config and ~/.gemini/GEMINI.md, and links skills into ~/.gemini/config/skills, so what other tools put there stays. A skill of the same name that another tool linked there is a conflict, as anywhere else. It does not support SSE servers. An sse server with an only list that names antigravity is an error in the config. An sse server without one goes to the other agents, is left out of Antigravity's file, and a machine that has agy says so in one warning line: warning Antigravity CLI does not support sse servers, so events is left out of ~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json Taking an agent's config off a machine Naming an agent out of a host file, or uninstalling it, only stops fleet from touching it. To remove what fleet put there: Take the agent's config out of the config repo for that machine: its settings.<agent> keys, the files records for its paths, and its servers (leave the name out of mcp.include, or take the agent out of the server's only). Run fleet push while the agent is still installed or named in agents. Apply removes the keys and links it recorded, and leaves what you made by hand. Then name the agents the machine keeps in its host file, such as agents: [claude], and push again. Fleet leaves the other agent alone from then on and stops warning about it. Do it in this order: a pinned-out agent is never touched, so a pin first would leave its files in place.

title: Setting up machines
heading: Servers
text: Servers The timer runs in a systemd user session. On a server, keep that session alive after you log out: sudo loginctl enable-linger <user> Without systemd, run fleet apply by hand or from cron.

title: Setting up machines
heading: The timer's schedule
text: The timer's schedule Every machine pulls and applies by itself every 30 minutes. timer: changes that: in hosts/_defaults.yaml for every machine, or in a host file for that one, the host file winning the way host files layer on the defaults. fleet status shows the schedule beside the timer's state. # hosts/_defaults.yaml timer: 30m # hosts/server.yaml timer: 10m # hosts/laptop.yaml timer: off Valid values are 5m, 10m, 15m, 20m, 30m, a whole hour 1h to 24h, and off; anything else is a config error naming them. These are the schedules both systems can express: Linux's timer runs OnUnitActiveSec at the interval, and on a Mac the LaunchAgent fires at the minutes or hours the schedule divides the hour or day into, so a run missed while the Mac slept happens when it wakes. timer: off leaves a machine to fleet push over ssh and manual applies: apply stops the timer and deletes the systemd unit or the LaunchAgent, so nothing is left running. Setting a value again turns the timer back on. Apply keeps the installed timer in step: when timer: changes, the next apply rewrites the unit or the plist and restarts it, and fleet diff lists the change like any other. fleet init installs the timer with the schedule the machine's config asks for. On a Mac, a change that the LaunchAgent's own run applies (the run every 30 minutes, for a Mac with no ssh:) is loaded once that run has finished: apply writes the new plist at once and a process of its own boots the agent out and in again afterwards, with its messages in ~/Library/Logs/fleet.log. Booting a running agent out from inside its own run would end that run and leave nothing loaded.

title: Setting up machines
heading: macOS
text: macOS Use macOS 12.3 or newer: the scripts use readlink -f. fleet init reads the version with sw_vers -productVersion and stops with a missing prerequisite on an older one. Install what fleet needs with Homebrew, on Apple Silicon (/opt/homebrew) or Intel (/usr/local): brew install node sops age xcode-select --install   # for git, if you have no other Fleet finds Homebrew's tools without a login shell, so the timer works without brew shellenv. On a Mac the timer is a LaunchAgent, ~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.github.rolfkoenders.fleet.apply.plist. It runs fleet apply when it loads (at login) and at the minutes or hours the machine's timer: divides the hour or day into (:00 and :30 each hour by default), and a run missed while the Mac slept happens when it wakes. The output goes to ~/Library/Logs/fleet.log. When that file passes 1 MB, the start of each apply cuts it down in place to its last 256 KB, at a line boundary. A log that is a symlink is left alone. Check it with fleet status, or launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/io.github.rolfkoenders.fleet.apply. A LaunchAgent runs only while its user is logged in at the desktop. fleet init over ssh to a Mac nobody is logged in to writes the file and stops with exit code 1, asking you to log in at the Mac, then run fleet init <host> again. Headless Macs, with nobody ever logged in, are out of scope: there is no timer for them. Two workarounds: turn on automatic login for the agent user, or leave the Mac without a timer and run fleet push from another machine over ssh to apply on it. Git must be able to read and push your config repo without a prompt, from a launchd job. A key kept in the macOS Keychain may need UseKeychain yes and AddKeysToAgent yes in ~/.ssh/config (Apple documents those two options). fleet init tests a push before it installs the timer, so a key the timer cannot use shows up there.

title: Setting up machines
heading: Machines that already have a setup
text: Machines that already have a setup fleet init ends with a first apply and then turns on the timer. Fleet stops at anything it did not write, lists it as a conflict, and writes nothing. Back up what you want to keep, clear each conflict, and run fleet init again. Init is safe to run as often as you need. fleet diff shows the same list without applying anything.

title: Setting up machines
heading: The age key
text: The age key Init prints the key of the machine you work from once, when it makes the key. That key opens every secret, so save it in your password manager. If an agent runs your commands, the printed key ends up in its session. Run this step yourself, or create the key first. Init then prints nothing: mkdir -p ~/.config/fleet age-keygen -o ~/.config/fleet/age.key chmod 600 ~/.config/fleet/age.key Init never prints the key of another machine. That key stays on that machine.

title: The bridge
heading: The bridge
text: fleet bridge opens a full-screen view of every host: a card each, the matrix of what each host gets, conflicts, the config's git history, secret names, the catalog, and each host's startup context. It needs a terminal. It reads, and the cards fill at once from what the last run saw, labelled "seen 2h ago, not live" until the host answers. That memory is ~/.local/state/fleet/bridge-hosts.json, which only the bridge reads and which holds no secrets. It keeps each host's startup context next to its status, cut to the fields the context screen shows.

title: The bridge
heading: Opening on a screen or a host
text: Opening on a screen or a host fleet bridge --view matrix --host server --view opens on a screen: home (the default), matrix, conflicts, timeline, secrets, catalog, push or context. These are the tabs, so a screen that gets a tab later gets a view. --host selects a host on that screen: its card on Home, its column in the Matrix, and its conflicts first on Conflicts. --host alone opens Home on that host's card. Both work in fleet demo's bridge. A name that is not one is refused with exit 2 before the screen is taken over, and the valid names are listed. --view push opens the push screen the way the 7 key does: nothing is reviewed or started until you press P.

title: The bridge
heading: Keys
text: Keys ? lists the keys, ctrl-k opens a palette, and r asks the hosts again. P reviews a push. Nothing runs until you type push and press enter. tab moves to an optional commit message (the same as fleet push -m); a message never starts a push. A push goes on by itself if you quit or the terminal closes, and the bridge waits for it when it can. h on the push screen opens the push history; enter replays the selected push, u undoes it after a confirmation, and esc goes back (see "The push journal"). d runs fleet doctor --json (--all across hosts) after you confirm. It starts real MCP servers with real credentials, so opening the bridge never does it. The result fills a health mark beside each server in the matrix; a server that only needs a login is shown as neutral, a server that rejected a configured secret is shown as failing, and any result the bridge does not know is shown as unknown.

title: The bridge
heading: Startup context
text: Startup context Tab 8 shows how much each agent on each host loads before its first prompt, as in fleet context --all: one stacked bar per host and agent (instructions, skills, MCP servers), all on one scale, so the heaviest host and agent are obvious. Under the bars are the selected host's parts and its largest items. ↑ and ↓ choose the host. An item fleet did not put there is marked not from config. A server nobody measured is shown as unknown, never as zero, and the agent's total ends in + because it is a lower bound; d measures the servers. Without colour the parts use █, ▓ and ░. Each home card has one line, context ~18.6k: the largest agent's total, with a + when a server is not measured. A host whose fleet is too old to have fleet context shows nothing there. The bridge asks each host for it by itself, together with the status: when it opens and on r, and again when a doctor run finishes, since the sizes just changed. For another host that is one more ssh call, fleet context --json. It reads files and starts no server, so it needs no confirmation, and doctor still runs only on d. What an earlier run saw is shown at once, marked "seen 2h ago, not live", until the host answers.

title: The bridge
heading: Pushing from the bridge
text: Pushing from the bridge A file that looks like a plaintext secret (.env, *.pem, *.key, names with secret or token) blocks a push from the bridge until you remove it or add it to .gitignore. fleet push itself does not check.

title: The bridge
heading: The push screen
text: The push screen While a push runs the pipeline row ends with the total time, and each lane ends with its own, running until its host is done. A host that is connecting over ssh says so from the start, with its time counting, instead of showing nothing. Below the lanes, the activity feed lists every event as it arrives, with its time and host. Beside it, the host pane shows the selected host: what it has written so far and how many writes remain, and after the push what it got, from the receipts in the push's end document (created, updated and removed, one line each; never a value). The pane follows the host being applied until you pick one with ↑ and ↓. The layout follows the width. From 100 columns everything shows. From 80 to 99 the host pane goes, and below 80 the feed goes too, leaving the lanes and the clock. The bridge itself needs at least 30 x 8. When the push is over, r on the selected lane runs fleet push --host <name>: it publishes as usual, then applies only on that host. A host without an ssh destination is refused with the reason. f on a lane with a conflict opens the Conflicts screen with that host first; it only shows the conflict and its fix.

title: The bridge
heading: The push journal
text: The push journal Every fleet push writes what it did to a file in ~/.local/state/fleet/pushes/ on the host that ran it, whether it was started from a terminal, from the bridge or with --host, and keeps the last 20 (older files are deleted when a new one is written). The file is named by its UTC start time and pid, such as 20261113T094103.123Z-4242.jsonl, and is private to you (mode 0600, in a 0700 directory). The first line is a header: the time, the commit pushed (the config repo's HEAD after publish, null when the push never got that far), which host --host named (or all), the hosts visited, how long it took, and how it ended. The other lines are the push's events as they arrived, each with t, the milliseconds since the push began. A push that is refused before it starts (locked, an unknown --host, an invalid config) writes nothing. A push that is cut short with ctrl-c keeps what it has and is marked interrupted. A journal that cannot be written is a message on stderr and never fails the push. The journal is never shared: each host has only its own, and fleet agent does not read it. There is no command for it. In the bridge, h on the push screen lists the recorded pushes, newest first, with time, scope (all hosts or the one host), result, duration and host count. enter replays the selected one at its real speed through the same screen a live push uses, so the clock, lanes, feed and host pane replay too; ↑ and ↓ pick a host as they do live, and esc goes back. u on the selected entry asks once, then runs fleet undo with --yes so it does not prompt again. When a push that ended ok is over, the bridge says how much faster or slower it was than the last earlier push of the same scope that also ended ok (1.4s faster than the last push), and leaves the line out when there is none.

title: The bridge
heading: Conflicts
text: Conflicts The conflicts screen lists every host's conflicts, read with fleet status --conflicts (read-only, no clone or fetch). A host on an older pin shows "detail needs a newer pin".

title: The bridge
heading: Look
text: Look The look is dark first. FLEET_THEME=light selects a best-effort palette for light terminals; it is less polished, and NO_COLOR and FLEET_NO_MOTION are honoured.

title: The bridge
heading: Trying it on made-up hosts
text: Trying it on made-up hosts fleet demo This builds a throwaway fleet in a temporary directory: three made-up hosts, a config repo, and local folders standing in for GitHub. On a terminal it opens the bridge on them, marked DEMO, with a conflict already waiting on server; press P to watch a push, or 8 to see the made-up startup context (devbox has a server nobody measured and a skill nobody configured). It needs only git and Node, touches nothing outside that directory, and deletes it when you quit. Without a terminal, or with --json, it runs a scripted walk-through itself and exits. fleet demo --shell gives a shell in the made-up fleet instead, with a printed list of commands to try.

title: The page
heading: The page
text: fleet ui starts a small web server inside the fleet process, prints its URL and opens your browser on it. The page shows this host, and pushes with live progress. It is a way to do from a browser what the bridge does in a terminal. Like the bridge, it is for you, not for an agent: fleet agent does not list it, and it has no --json form. fleet ui                  # a free port, opens the browser fleet ui --port 8765      # a fixed port fleet ui --no-open        # print the URL and do not open a browser It stops on ctrl-c, or by itself after 10 minutes with no page open. A push or a host set-up that is running when you press ctrl-c is its own process and finishes without the page; the terminal says so and points at fleet status. For a host set-up it also says that nothing will remove the host file if init fails. Reload, and when the server goes away Reload is safe. The token is kept in sessionStorage, which belongs to that tab alone (it is never in the address or the history after the page loads, and no other tab sees it). So F5 keeps the page working. The To push list is kept there too and comes back after a reload: it holds only edits, and an edit never holds a plain secret value (a value goes to the server once, in its own request, and the edit is sops ciphertext). While a push or a host set-up runs, the browser asks before the tab is closed or reloaded. A tab that joins mid-run catches up. The server tells every new page which jobs run (a push, fleet init of a host, a clone, a check, a secret being encrypted) and replays the last events of the running push or init, so a second tab or a reload shows the lanes and log so far, and labels the job correctly (a host set-up is not shown as a push). The header names every running job. Not answering. If fleet ui stopped, was restarted, or this machine slept, the header says not answering and a banner says what to do: run fleet ui again and open the new URL in the same tab. Push, Add and Set value are off meanwhile, and the page keeps trying. Token no longer valid. If the server answers but refuses the page's token, it was started again. The page stops retrying (a refused token never becomes valid), says so, and the To push list is restored when you open the new URL in the same tab. A new tab without the URL cannot do anything, as before.

title: The page
heading: What is on the page
text: What is on the page A header with this host, its checkout and whether the live connection is up (it reconnects by itself if the server drops it), and a menu: Matrix, Catalog, Hosts, Secrets, Card, Review & push and Status. The page is plain files under src/ui/static/ that fleet serves as they are: no build step, no framework and no dependency, and nothing is loaded from another origin, including its font (JetBrains Mono, bundled in src/ui/static/fonts/ with its licence, a copy of the landing page's). Matrix The first screen, named like the bridge's Matrix screen and read the same way. One row per skill bundle and per MCP server, one column per host. A bundle row opens to show its skills, which are read-only. A cell says where the item comes from for that host: Cell Meaning ✓ default the defaults give it + added the host's own file adds it ✕ excluded the host (or the defaults) excludes it · off nothing picks it Clicking a cell makes the smallest edit to that host's file, as a change to push: an item the defaults give is taken away with exclude in the host's file (the defaults are not edited), an item the host added is taken out of its list, an exclude is taken back. Clicking the same cell again takes that edit back. Hovering a cell says what a click will do: give, take away or undo. A host's name is a button that shows its file in the pane beside the table, as it will be written, with comments, blank lines and list style kept; nothing is on disk yet. The + Add button in the header offers what the Catalog's does, plus a host. A server, skill source or bundle you add is a row of the Matrix at once, off for every host, held like any edit. Search The Matrix and the Catalog each start with a search field that filters their rows (or cards) by name as you type, without regard to case. A bundle also matches when one of its skills does (a source matches by the skills fleet has read from it too): on the Matrix its row says skill review when that is why it is shown, and its matching skills are highlighted when it is open. / goes to the field, unless you are typing in another field or a dialog is open. Esc clears the field, and blurs it when it is already empty. The filter is part of the page address, as a query of the screen (#/matrix?q=git), so a reload keeps it and the address can be copied. The token is handled as before. Opening another screen from the menu starts without a filter. It only hides rows. To push and Review & push are never filtered. When the filter hides rows that have an edit on To push, the field says so (2 hidden with changes, with their names as its tooltip). A filter that matches nothing says so and has a Clear the filter button. Catalog The MCP servers, skill sources and skill bundles your hosts can pick from. The + Add button in the header offers an MCP server, a skill source or a skill bundle, and so does the dashed tile at the end of each section. Adding one gives it to no host: pick it in the Matrix. An addition is a change to push, so it shows in Review & push like a pick does, and one that is on To push has a Remove from push button (which takes back the picks of it too). Each choice opens a dialog (a native modal <dialog>): focus goes to its first field and stays inside (Tab wraps), the page behind does not scroll, and Esc or Cancel closes it and leaves nothing behind, no edit to push and no form state, so it opens blank next time. Enter in a field does what the main button does. Beside the form the dialog shows the YAML that will be written as a diff against the file (catalog/mcp.yaml or catalog/skills.yaml), asked from the server as you type, so it is the server's own splice and not a copy of its rules. Every rule below is the server's and is also checked by the page before the click, in the same words. While the input is not valid yet, the pane lists what is still missing instead. Add to push puts the edit on To push and closes the dialog. On a phone the dialog fills the screen and the diff stacks under the form. An MCP server. A name, whether it runs on the machine (a command) or at a URL (http or sse), the environment (or, for a URL, headers) as a plain value or secret:NAME, and which agents get it (the boxes are the agents this machine has, another machine last reported through the bridge, or a host file names; "Show all agents" reveals the rest, and an agent that is not shown keeps its value, so hiding it never narrows the server to fewer agents). A secret can never be in the command (the loader's rule, with its message), and a command such as npx pkg or uvx pkg with no version gets a warning and can still be held. A URL holds no credentials (user:pw@) and no space: put them in headers as secret:NAME. A row with a value and no name is told to give it a name. A name is at most 64 characters, and names compare without regard to case (WEB1 next to web1 is refused, because a source is a directory of that name and some tools lower-case a server's). An addition already on To push says already added to To push. Check it starts. Runs doctor's probe on the one server you are adding, on this machine, and shows its tools and their size in tokens. It asks first, naming the command: it runs with the real credentials fleet can read for this host and may download packages. A secret that has no value on this host is left out and named, so the server starts without it. Nothing is written. A skill source. A name, a repo (a URL, an scp-style address or a path on this machine), a path and an optional branch. Look at the repo clones it shallowly into a temp directory, lists its skills and reads its head commit. A pinned source (the default) is written with that commit, track for the branch and review: true; a followed one with its branch. A repo has no credentials in it (user:pw@, or a token as the user of an https URL): use a git credential helper or an ssh key; the page and the server refuse it, and an error that echoes a URL shows it without its userinfo. The repo, branch and path are checked before Look at the repo, which stays off while one is wrong, and a clone that fails is shown as an error under the button. The temp clone is deleted when you close the dialog, when a newer one replaces it and when the server stops. A bundle. A name and its skills, picked from the sources fleet has cloned and from a source you hold, or typed in. Edit Every card on the Catalog (MCP server, skill source, skill bundle) and on Hosts has an Edit button next to its YAML toggle. The Matrix has none. Edit opens the Add dialog of that kind with the current values filled in, titled Edit ..., with the same live YAML diff and checks. The name is read-only, because renaming would leave host files pointing at nothing. Save to push puts the edit on To push, where it shows in Review & push like any other, and Remove from push on the card undoes it. Esc and Cancel close the dialog and leave nothing behind. What each dialog changes. An MCP server: everything the Add dialog has except the name (command or URL, kind, environment or headers, which agents). A skill bundle: its skills. A skill source: path, branch, whether it is pinned or followed, and review; the repo is read-only, because a changed repo would break the clones machines already have (a source's clone is kept under its name and its origin is never reset), so another repo is another source. A host: its ssh destination only; its bundles and servers stay on the Matrix, and admin, age, vars, settings and files stay hand-written. Only what changed is written. An edit holds each field it changes with what the file held before (from) and what it should hold (to). Every other key and comment in the file and in the entry stays byte for byte; a changed value keeps the comment at the end of its line, a cleared field is removed with its line, and a new key is placed where the entry writes its keys. A list of skills changes by line: a skill that goes loses its line, a new one follows the one before it, and the rest keep their comments. The result is read again and must be exactly the old document with the changes made. Secrets. A secret:NAME row shows the name, and can be switched between a secret and a plain value. A value is never shown or sent: setting one stays on the Secrets page, and a name that has no value on a host shows the same tag as in Add. A field that is as the file has it is not checked again. A rule the file may have been written without (a {{ vars.NAME }} in a URL, a variable name Add would not offer, an unpinned command) does not block an edit of another field. A field that changes is checked as in Add. A skill source. Changing only the path or review leaves the pin where it is and needs no clone. Changing the branch, or switching between pinned and followed, looks at the repo first, as Add does (a shallow clone in a temp directory, deleted when the dialog closes): a pinned source moves its commit to the head of the new branch, and the dialog says so (The pin moves to 1a2b3c4, the head of dev) and lists the skills found. An unpushed addition is changed in place. Editing an item whose addition is still on To push changes that addition. An edit of an item is also changed in place: the dialog starts from the file with the held edit on top, and when it is put back to what the file says, saving takes the edit off To push. Stale edits. If the file says something else for a field at write time, the edit is dropped with a clear message ('servers.docs.command' is not what this edit was made from: it has changed in the file), Review & push lists it and holds the push until you forget it, and the newer value is never overwritten. Entries fleet cannot change safely. Anchors, aliases, tags, flow maps for an entry, a flow list over several lines, block text (|, >), items not on lines of their own and Windows line endings are refused by the engine rather than guessed at. The button stays: Edit opens a dialog that shows the item's lines read-only, the reason, and the file to edit by hand. An anchor or alias anywhere in a file makes every entry in that file read-only, because the engine reads the whole file. Remove Every card on the Catalog (MCP server, skill source, skill bundle) and on Hosts has a Remove button next to Edit and YAML. The Matrix has none. It opens a dialog (a native modal <dialog>, like Add and Edit) that says what will change and shows the YAML diff of every file touched; nothing is staged or run until its button is pressed. Esc and Cancel close it and leave nothing behind. An MCP server or a bundle is taken out of its catalog entry and out of every reference to it: mcp.include and mcp.exclude for a server, bundles and exclude for a bundle, in hosts/_defaults.yaml and in each host file. The dialog lists every host (and the defaults) it touches. The removal goes on To push as one held edit, so the config still loads for every host after it, and Remove from push on the item's card (drawn dimmed, tagged removal to push, while the removal is held) undoes it as a unit. A skill source is taken out of the catalog, and its skills out of every bundle that lists them. The dialog says what each bundle loses (core loses 3 skills). A bundle left with no skills is kept, as [] (the config allows it), and is flagged in the dialog and on its card (no skills). Which skills a source provides is what the page knows of it: its clone on this machine, or what it saw when the source was added; a skill that another source also provides stays. When the page cannot tell (no clone here), the dialog says so, and bundles keep their skills. The clone of the source on each machine is left alone. An item whose addition is still on To push is not staged for removal: removing it drops the addition, and every edit or pick of it that was held. Nothing is written. The edits that name the item (a host's pick of it, an Edit of it) are dropped when the removal is held, because they would be stale after it; the dialog lists them. What goes with the entry. The entry's own lines go, with the comments inside it and the comment lines right above it (the lines the YAML view shows for the item), and the blank line that set it apart. Every other comment and blank line, in the catalog and in the host files, stays byte for byte. A section left with no entry is written as {}, which the loader reads as empty, and an Add writes into it again. Stale. If the item is already gone from the file at write time, or the file has a shape the engine refuses, the removal is dropped with a clear message ('docs' is not in catalog/mcp.yaml), Review & push lists it and holds the push until you forget it, and nothing is written. A host is removed at once after you confirm, like adding one, not through To push. The server takes the push lock, deletes hosts/<name>.yaml and secrets/<name>.enc.yaml (if there), runs the real fleet secrets rekey as a child process (so .sops.yaml and the shared secrets file stop naming its key), then commits (Remove host <name>) and pushes the config repo. Its output is streamed into the page as it comes. When rekey or the commit fails, every file is put back and nothing is committed; when only the push fails, the commit stays and the page says to push it. The edits on To push for that host (its picks, its ssh edit, and a secret set for shared or for it, which the rekey makes stale) are dropped, and the dialog lists them. It refuses, like adding a host, while a push runs and while the config repo has changes the page did not make. What the host dialog says. The machine keeps its files, and its timer will report errors until fleet is turned off there. It lists the secret names the host could read (those in shared, when it has a key, and those in its own file; names only, never a value) and says to change them: rekeying changes who can read the files, not the secrets' values. Refused: for the host the page runs on, and for the only admin host (admin: true). The button is disabled with the reason as its title, and the server refuses the same. YAML Every MCP server, skill source and skill bundle on the Catalog, and every host on Hosts, has a YAML button (a toggle: aria-pressed, reachable and operable by keyboard). On, the card opens to show how the item is written in the config repo: its own lines in catalog/mcp.yaml or catalog/skills.yaml, with the comments right above it, or for a host the whole of hosts/<name>.yaml, under the file's path and in the same code style as the diffs. It is read-only and shows only what is literally in the file, so a secret is secret:NAME and never a value. When the item has an edit on To push (an addition, or a host file changed by a pick in the Matrix), the panel shows the diff of its lines against the repo instead, tagged to push: +N -M. Show all YAML in the header opens or closes every card of the screen at once. A screen reads the files again whenever it is opened. Hosts One card per host: how it is reached, and what it gets. + Add host, in the header and as the tile after the cards, opens a dialog that sets up a new machine from the page. Like the Catalog's, it is modal, takes focus, closes on Esc or Cancel with nothing written, and shows the host file that will be written (hosts/<name>.yaml, a new file) as a diff while you type, or what is still missing. Esc and Cancel are off while fleet init runs, because the run goes on without the page; after it ends, a failure keeps the form to try again and a success is closed with Done. A name (the loader's rule for a host name), an ssh destination and where it starts from: the defaults only, or a copy of another host. ssh is required, because fleet init refuses a host without it; for a machine fleet cannot reach over ssh the form links setting up machines. A destination that starts with -, or has a space or another symbol, is refused, and so is one with no host after the @ (bob@) or with a port (bob@mini:22): set Port for the host in ~/.ssh/config instead. A name is at most 64 characters, shared is reserved (it is the secrets file every host reads), and a name that differs from a host only in case is refused, because on some disks it is the same file; the file is created only when nothing is there, so a failed init never removes a file it did not make. A copy takes bundles, exclude, mcp, settings and vars of the other host, with the comments inside them, and not its ssh, age or files. This is not a change to push. After you confirm (the page names the machine and what will run there), the server takes the push lock, writes hosts/<name>.yaml with the edit engine and runs the real fleet init <name> as a child process, so it commits and pushes itself (the host file, .sops.yaml and the re-encrypted secrets), exactly as from the CLI. Its output is streamed into the page as it comes: one line when each step starts and one when it ends, under a running clock (the page sets FLEET_INIT_PROGRESS=1 for the child; run from a terminal, fleet init prints its report at the end as always, and --json is unchanged). It refuses while there are changes to push (the page asks you to push or discard them first, so init's commit does not sweep them in), while a push runs, while the config repo has changes the page did not make, and for a host that already exists. When init fails before it committed anything, the host file is deleted and the files init rewrote are restored, so the repo is as it was. When init had already committed and pushed (for example the timer step failed on the host), the host file stays, because that commit is published; the page says so, and fleet init <name> finishes the rest when run again. Removing a host is on its card: see Remove. Secrets A table of every secret name against every host, by name only. A cell is set (the host's own secrets file has the name, or shared has it and the host can read shared), missing (a server the host picks, or its settings, use the name and neither file has it) or not used. A value to push shows as set with to push, and the tab counts the missing cells. Set value (Replace value when it is set everywhere it is needed) opens a password field: A value of more than 8192 characters, or of only spaces, is refused with the limit named; the field never cuts what is typed. Typing a value here is allowed. It is sent to the server once, over the page's own connection, and is never logged, echoed, kept or sent back. The field is not named (a password manager does not offer to save it), asks for no autofill, and is emptied before the request goes; the page holds no copy of it in its state, storage or address. The value is encrypted at once: the server copies the host's secrets file into a private temp directory (mode 0700), runs sops set --value-stdin there (the value goes on sops' stdin, never in argv or the environment) and reads the new file back. The directory is removed whatever happens, and the repo is not touched. The result is a change to push that carries the encrypted file, shown in Review & push by its names with a short mark of each ciphertext. It is checked as strictly as a pick: the path must be a secrets file of shared or of a host with an age recipient, the text must hold nothing but ciphertext, it must be encrypted for exactly the recipients .sops.yaml names for that file, and it may add or replace only the names it says (no delete, no rename). It is written over the file it was made from only: when that file changed on disk since, the edit is dropped as stale and nothing is overwritten, and you set the value again. It goes to the hosts that pick a server using the secret and do not have it yet, unticked others can be added, and shared is a choice of its own. A host with no age key cannot be chosen. A failure is one of a few fixed sentences. What sops said is never passed on, because it can quote what it was given. This sets and replaces. It does not delete or rename a secret: use fleet secrets for that. Card An image of your fleet to share: in a post, a GitHub discussion, or a README. It is an image because terminal text loses its colours the moment it leaves the terminal. The same card comes from fleet card, which writes fleet-card.svg (1200 x 630, the social preview size) in the current folder; the page shows what that command would write. Two styles, switched at the top of the screen (fleet card --style machines|map, machines is the default). *Machines* has the four counts large (machines, agents, skills, MCP servers), a row per machine with its agents as badges and its OS, and a bottom line: N changes in the last year · N pushes since March 2026. *Map* puts the config in the middle and each machine as a card around it, with its agents, its OS and when it last applied (linux · 4m ago), and skills and MCP servers on the left of the bottom line, changes and pushes on the right. Above 6 machines the map shows 6 and a +N more card; machines shows 6 rows and +N more. The activity grid. *Machines* shows a GitHub-style grid of the config repo's commits per day, five shades of green, but only when the repo had at least 20 commits in the last 12 months. Below that it is left out and only the bottom line stays, because an empty grid looks like a dead setup. The map has no grid. What is counted. A change is a commit to the config repo, read from its git log. Pushes are the ones in this host's push journal, which keeps only the last 20, so a full journal reads 20+ pushes. The month is the one of the config repo's first commit. Skills and MCP servers are the ones some host gets, each counted once, and agents are counted once across hosts. Privacy. Hosts are host 1, host 2 and so on, in name order, unless Show hostnames is on (--names in the CLI). The names of MCP servers, skills, skill sources and secrets are never on the card, with or without it, and neither is the startup context. Nothing asks a host. Agents, OS and the last apply of each host are what the bridge last saw of it (the answers it keeps in ~/.local/state/fleet/bridge-hosts.json), and this host is read live, so the card works offline and without ssh. A host the bridge never saw is drawn without agents and OS, and the page says how many (never which, unless names are on): run fleet bridge once to read them. Save PNG draws the card on a canvas at twice its size (2400 x 1260) and downloads it. The server draws the SVG, with the same code as the CLI, and the page only turns it into a PNG. Copy image puts that PNG on the clipboard; a browser that refuses (it needs a secure page and its permission, which 127.0.0.1 counts as) gets a plain message and Save PNG is the way round. Save SVG downloads the file fleet card writes. Post to Show and tell opens a new discussion in the Show and tell category of the project with a short title and text filled in (counts only, no hostname), in a new tab: you attach the image yourself. Fonts. The SVG file names JetBrains Mono and then the monospace faces every system has (Fira Code, SF Mono, Menlo, Consolas, DejaVu Sans Mono), and Geist for the big counts, falling back to the same monospace. It embeds no font and fetches nothing, so it reads anywhere. The picture on this page and the PNG carry the bundled JetBrains Mono inside them, so they look as designed whatever is installed. The README badge. fleet card --badge writes fleet-badge.svg, a small badge (fleet · 3 machines · 3 agents) in the same colours, for a config repo's README: !fleet. It holds no hostname. Before it writes the file, fleet card prints what is on it, so you see what you are about to publish: $ fleet card   ● fleet   3 machines · 3 agents · 38 skills · 9 MCP servers    host 1  claude opencode   linux   host 2  claude            linux   host 3  claude agy        macos    activity, 12 months  ▁▂▁▃▅▂▁▁▂▆▇▃▂▁▃▂▁▅▃▂▂▁▁▃▇█▅▂▁▂▃▂▁▁▂▃▅▃▂▁▂▆▃▂▁▃▂▅▇▃▂▃    412 changes this year · 128 pushes since March 2026 · hostnames hidden  wrote fleet-card.svg (1200 x 630) The activity line follows the same 20-commit rule. The page shows this text under the picture. Review & push The real diff of every file the changes to push change. A check per host: whether its config loads with the edits (the same load fleet push starts with, and a host that would fail shows its problems), and its pick changes worked out from the config, such as + skills notes, deploy; − server docs. This host only: the full plan, from fleet diff run on the edited config. It is worked out in memory and writes nothing. Other hosts are not planned, because that needs ssh; they get the pick summary instead. A commit message, suggested from the edits and yours to change. Write and push writes the files, commits them with the message, runs the real fleet push and shows each host's lane as it goes. Discard all drops the changes to push; until you push, nothing has touched the disk. The page holds the edits as operations (add or remove of a bundle or server for a host, and addServer, addSource and addBundle for the catalog). The server rebuilds each from the fields it may have and checks an entry with the loader's own code, so the page can add nothing the loader would refuse. Every preview replays them, through the edit engine in src/edit/, on the files as they are on disk at that moment. An edit that no longer applies (the file changed under it) is listed as dropped with its reason, and nothing is written while any is. Changes the page did not make. When the config repo has uncommitted changes of its own (git status --porcelain), the page lists them and refuses to write or push until you commit or discard them outside the page. The server checks again right before writing, so a change made after the page last looked is still caught. The server also refuses, before writing anything, while a push is running (a push is already running (pid N)), when an edit is stale, and when the edited config would not load for a host.

title: The page
heading: API
text: API Every route is JSON under /api/ and sits behind the checks below. Request bodies are used, never logged. Route Does GET /api/status what fleet status --json knows about this host GET /api/matrix hosts, bundles with their skills, servers, and each host's cell; plus outside, the uncommitted changes in the config repo GET /api/secrets secret names and who can read them, and table: each name against each host as set, missing or unused, never a value POST /api/secrets/set {name, value, files, ops}: encrypts one value into the secrets file of each of files (shared or a host) with sops in a private temp dir, and answers the setSecret edits to push that carry those files. Nothing is written to the repo, and the value is in no answer, error, log or event; 400 invalid, 409 stale, 422 no-recipient, needs-secret, sops-failed, recipients or invalid GET /api/skills the skills in the source clones fleet already has, and the bundle that holds each; nothing is cloned or fetched POST /api/catalog/clone {repo, path?, branch?}: a shallow clone in a temp directory; answers its id, head commit, branch and skills. The repo must be a URL, an scp-style address or an absolute path, never something git reads as an option, and goes after -- POST /api/catalog/discard {id}: deletes that temp clone POST /api/catalog/probe {name, entry, confirm: true}: doctor's probe on one entry that is not on disk, on this machine; refused unless confirm is true. Answers result, tools, tokens and unset (secret names with no value here), never a value POST /api/preview {ops, show?, staged?}: the files the edits change (before and after), dropped edits, the matrix after, a check per host. A host also fails its check when it gets a bundle that names a skill no source provides, as fleet push would find; that check uses the skills of the clones on this machine and of staged (the skills of sources just added, by source name), and says nothing while a source's skills are not known POST /api/card {style?, names?} with style machines or map: the card, drawn by the same code as fleet card from what fleet last saw of each host (nothing is asked over ssh): svg, badge, text (the terminal preview), unseen (how many hosts the bridge never saw) and share (title, body, url of a new Show and tell discussion). Hostnames only with names: true; 400 for another style POST /api/yaml {kind, name} with kind server, source, bundle or host: the file that item is written in, as on disk, as {path, text} (the catalog file, or hosts/<name>.yaml). It takes a kind and a name, never a path; a bad name is 400, a host that is not there 404. Secrets files are not reachable, and the files hold only secret:NAME, never a value POST /api/entry {ops, kind, name} with kind server, source, bundle or host: what an Edit dialog starts from, the item as the files would have it after the held ops. Answers found, value (the entry as written: a bundle's skills, a host's {ssh}, a secret as secret:NAME), path, editable, reason when it cannot be edited in place, and text, the file it is in POST /api/plan {ops}: this host's plan from fleet diff on the edited config POST /api/hosts/preview {name, ssh, from?}: the host file /api/hosts/init would write, as {path, before, after}; needs no confirmation, writes and runs nothing; 400 invalid, 409 stale for a host that exists POST /api/hosts/init {name, ssh, from?, confirm: true}: writes hosts/<name>.yaml and runs the real fleet init, streaming its output as init events and answering when it ends; 409 locked, outside-changes or exists, 422 invalid POST /api/hosts/remove/preview {name}: what removing the host changes: files (its host file, its own secrets file by names only, and .sops.yaml as rekey will write it), rekeyed, and readable (the secret NAMES it could read, shared and own). Writes and runs nothing; 409 self, admin or stale POST /api/hosts/remove {name, confirm: true}: deletes the host's files, runs the real fleet secrets rekey, commits and pushes, streaming its output as remove events and answering when it ends (removed, kept when only the push failed); 409 locked, outside-changes, self, admin or stale POST /api/write {ops, message}: writes, commits, then pushes; 409 locked, outside-changes or stale, 422 invalid POST /api/push runs fleet push with what is already committed GET /api/events the stream of live push events, and of init and remove output. It starts with hello (pushing, and jobs: what runs, each {kind, name?} with kind push, init, remove, clone, check or secret), then replays the events of a running push, init or removal (the last 400), then sends jobs whenever the list changes

title: The page
heading: Who can reach it
text: Who can reach it The page can change your config and push, so nothing but you may reach it. It listens on 127.0.0.1 only. There is no option to listen elsewhere. The URL is http://127.0.0.1:<port>/#t=<token>: a random port and a random token. The page reads the token from the part after # (which a browser never sends to the server), keeps it in memory (and in sessionStorage of that tab, so a reload works) and sends it as a header on every call. There is no cookie. Opening the URL without the token shows a page that cannot do anything. A request whose Host is not 127.0.0.1:<port> is refused, so a web page on another site cannot reach the server by pointing its own name at your machine (DNS rebinding). A write whose Origin is not the page itself is refused too. The server sends no CORS header, so no other page can read an answer. Its pages may show images from the page itself and from blob: (the card, drawn into a canvas), and nothing from another origin. The one call that cannot carry a header is the stream of live updates (a browser's EventSource cannot), so that call takes the token in its query instead. Nothing logs a URL. A secret's value is never sent to the browser. Nothing the page sends is logged, and the one route that takes a value (/api/secrets/set) answers with the encrypted file and fixed messages only.

title: The page
heading: Pushing
text: Pushing A push from the page (and the one after Write and push) runs the real fleet push, so it takes the same push lock as a push from a terminal or the bridge. While another push is running, the page shows a push is already running (pid N) and starts nothing.

title: The page
heading: On a server
text: On a server With SSH_CONNECTION set, fleet does not try to open a browser. The URL is printed, and you reach it from your own machine through a tunnel: ssh -L 8765:127.0.0.1:8765 <the host>     # on your machine fleet ui --port 8765 --no-open            # on the host Then open the printed URL (with the same port) on your machine.

title: MCP logins
heading: Logging in to MCP servers
text: Fleet writes each server's entry, not your login. A server that uses OAuth needs one login per machine and per tool. Tool How to log in Claude Code /mcp in a session opencode opencode mcp auth <name> Antigravity CLI Not from the CLI. See Antigravity CLI

title: MCP logins
heading: Logging in on a machine you reach over SSH
text: Logging in on a machine you reach over SSH After you log in, the browser redirects to a localhost port. That port has to reach the machine running the login, so connect with a tunnel and start the login from that session. Port 19876 is the one opencode uses: ssh -L 19876:127.0.0.1:19876 server opencode mcp auth <name> Open the printed link in the browser on your own machine.

title: MCP logins
heading: Servers on plain HTTP
text: Servers on plain HTTP Claude Code refuses to send OAuth credentials to a plain HTTP address unless it is on localhost. A server on your local network needs an HTTPS address before you can log in to it.

title: MCP logins
heading: Antigravity CLI
text: Antigravity CLI Antigravity's documentation describes the login for an OAuth server in the Antigravity app only (Customizations, Installed, MCP Servers, Authenticate), not in the CLI. The CLI's /mcp panel shows each server's status, reloads the config and shows the connection log, so use it to see whether a server connected. The app keeps the tokens in ~/.gemini/antigravity/mcp_oauth_tokens.json, and the documentation does not say whether the CLI reads that file. Check it for your server before you rely on it. A server that takes a static header needs no login: put the header in the catalog entry (headers, with secret:NAME for the value). Antigravity passes $VAR and ${VAR} in env and headers on as written, so put the value itself in the secret. If fleet doctor reports bad-auth for such a server, the server answered HTTP 401 or 403 with that secret. The doctor output names the secret, which secrets file holds it, and when that file's git history last changed the secret's ciphertext. Set a new value with fleet secrets set or in the Secrets screen of fleet ui. Fleet does not write oauth or authProviderType into the entry. Antigravity does not support SSE servers, so an sse server is left out of its file (see Setting up machines).

title: Adding an agent
heading: Adding an agent
text: What fleet knows about an agent is one module in src/agents/ and one line in the registry. Nothing else names an agent: the rest of the tool loops over the registry. Antigravity CLI (src/agents/antigravity.ts) was added this way and is the example to read next to this page.

title: Adding an agent
heading: What an agent has to be
text: What an agent has to be An agent is accepted when all of these hold: It keeps its configuration in user-level files fleet can merge: a settings file, an MCP file, instructions or a skills directory under the user's home. An agent that is configured only in a cloud console, an app database or per project does not fit. It is maintained: it has releases, and its documentation is current. It installs on Linux and macOS, with a program on the path (or in a directory its installer uses, or one of the shim directories fleet searches, such as mise's) that prints a version. It is documented: the official documentation says where each file is and what its keys mean. Fleet cannot check a path against the code, so the module cites the page.

title: Adding an agent
heading: The steps
text: The steps Read the documentation, then the real agent. Install it in a throwaway home (HOME=$(mktemp -d)) and look at what it reads and writes. Never run it against your own home to find out. Write src/agents/<id>.ts. It exports an Agent (see src/agents/types.ts): an id that host files will use (renaming it later breaks every config), a name, the binary, the arguments that print its version, and homes, the paths that belong to it alone. Then the optional parts it has: settings: the file the agent also writes, and denied, the dotted paths no config may own (what the agent writes itself, account and credential keys, keys it ignores). mcp: the file, the key the servers are under, render for the entry of a server in the agent's shape, read for the way back (doctor uses it), skip for an entry the agent does not load, and transports when it cannot take all of stdio, http and sse. skills: the directory fleet links skills into, and every directory the agent reads, lowest precedence first. instructions: the files and directories it reads as instructions. Cite the documentation in a comment for every path, key and format the module uses: one URL per fact, so a reviewer can check it. A path or key with no source is not merged. Add one line to AGENTS in src/agents/index.ts, last, because the order is the order fleet lists agents in. The compiler then asks for the rest: the demo's version line in src/demo/fakes.ts. The demo's machines have only the agents in DEMO_AGENTS (src/demo/sandbox.ts) installed, so a new agent is not on them unless you add it there. Run the conformance suite. test/agents.conformance.test.ts runs against every registered agent: identity, MCP render and read for each transport, denied keys refused as they are, below them and above them, the location checks, and an apply followed by taking everything away in a temp home. It needs no edit to cover the new agent. An agent whose MCP writes must go through its own binary needs a fake of its own in FAKES; most need none, because the suite installs a fake that prints a version. Add the agent's own tests for what is particular to it (test/antigravity.test.ts): the shape of its entries, the keys it refuses, a host without it. List it. Add it to the Supported agents lists in README.md and site/index.html, to the term Agent in GLOSSARY.md and in src/agent.ts (a test keeps the two equal), and give examples/hosts/_defaults.yaml the link of the shared instructions into its file. The list in fleet agent comes from the registry. Add a line to CHANGELOG.md under ## Unreleased.

title: Adding an agent
heading: Checking it
text: Checking it npm run typecheck npm test Then apply the example config in a temp HOME with the real agent on the path and ask the agent itself what it sees: HOME=<tmp> agy mcp list lists the servers fleet wrote, for example. If the agent only reads a file once you sign in, say so in the pull request and show what you could check. Never run fleet apply, fleet init or the agent against your real home while you work on this.

title: Adding an agent
heading: What review looks at
text: What review looks at Every path, key and format has a documentation link, and the link says what the comment claims. homes hold only what is the agent's: a folder shared with another tool (Antigravity CLI and Gemini CLI both use ~/.gemini) is listed by the files and directories that are the agent's alone. denied has what the agent writes itself, so a config cannot own a key the agent keeps rewriting. A host without the agent is unchanged: no file written, no word in diff, apply or status. Nothing in the module makes this so: for every agent, fleet names it only on a host that has it installed, pins it in agents:, or has applied config for it. Config that already exists keeps working after the agent is registered. If the new agent cannot take something existing config says (an sse server for every agent), it leaves it out and says so, and does not turn the config into an error.

title: FAQ
heading: Where do my secrets end up?
text: Where do my secrets end up? They are encrypted in secrets/ in your config repo. On apply, fleet decrypts the ones a machine needs and writes them in plaintext into the settings files of your agents, at mode 600, because the tools read them from there.

title: FAQ
heading: What if I lose the age key?
text: What if I lose the age key? Nobody can read the secrets without a key that can decrypt them, and the key of the machine you work from is the only one that opens all of them. Keep it in your password manager.

title: FAQ
heading: Does fleet touch skills or settings it did not write?
text: Does fleet touch skills or settings it did not write? No. It leaves other entries in ~/.claude/skills alone, and in a settings file it changes only the keys your config names. If something is already at a path fleet wants to write, that is a conflict, and fleet stops.

title: FAQ
heading: Why does fleet say an agent is not installed?
text: Why does fleet say an agent is not installed? A machine gets the agents installed on it, and fleet found none of <agent> although it applied config for it on this machine earlier. (An agent that was never set up here is not mentioned, however much the config says about it.) It leaves everything of that agent alone until it is installed, and says so on each apply, diff and status. If the machine should not have the agent at all, name the agents it keeps in its host file: agents: [claude]. See setting up machines, which also covers removing an agent's config.

title: FAQ
heading: When does a change reach a machine?
text: When does a change reach a machine? fleet push applies it straight away on every machine with an ssh: line in its host file. Every machine also pulls and applies on its own timer, every 30 minutes by default, so one that was offline catches up. timer: in hosts/_defaults.yaml changes the schedule for every machine and in a host file for that one; timer: off leaves a machine to fleet push and manual applies, and apply installs, changes and removes the timer to match. A machine with no ssh: line gets changes only this way.

title: FAQ
heading: What does the install script do?
text: What does the install script do? It checks for git and Node, clones the tool into ~/.local/share/fleet/fleet, and links fleet into ~/.local/bin. It uses no sudo and installs nothing else, and you can read it first. Running it again changes nothing.

title: FAQ
heading: How do I update fleet?
text: How do I update fleet? Your machines run the tool commit pinned in fleet.yaml, so a new version reaches them only when you choose to take it. fleet update moves the pin to the newest release and prints what changed; a major version is flagged, and its "You need to do" section is the one to read first. If track: in fleet.yaml names a branch instead of releases, it moves to that branch's latest commit. Read the output and git diff, then run fleet push.

title: FAQ
heading: Should I work in ~/.local/share/fleet/fleet?
text: Should I work in ~/.local/share/fleet/fleet? No. That is the copy your machine runs, and fleet moves it to the pinned commit. To work on the tool, use a separate checkout and run its own bin/fleet.

title: FAQ
heading: Does it run on macOS?
text: Does it run on macOS? Yes, macOS 12.3 or newer. The timer is a LaunchAgent instead of a systemd timer, and the scripts and tool search know Homebrew. See macOS.
